strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: multi-frame spatial understanding in MLLMs, whereas prior spatial data efforts (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT) are single-image. The claim of being the first large-scale multi-frame spatial dataset is credible given the related-work comparison in Table 1.

The data engine is technically sound and well described: back-projecting aligned point clouds to establish pixel correspondences, overlap-ratio-based balanced pair sampling with long-tail mitigation, BFS-based minimum-coverage-set search for object size data, and clustering-based rigid body segmentation for dynamic data. These are concrete, reproducible contributions beyond simple QA generation.

The benchmark covers 26 subtasks across five task categories with diverse referencing (dots, coordinates, semantic labels) and output formats (qualitative, MCQ, scalar, vector, coordinate), with a held-out scene split to prevent scene leakage between train and eval.

Results are convincing: large gains over InternVL2 base models across all subtasks (avg +35.68), outperformance of GPT-4o/Gemini-2.0/Claude-3.5 on most subtasks with an 8B model, and zero-shot transfer to BLINK (+26.4 avg over base, near 90% on Visual Correspondence and Multi-View Reasoning), which supports generalization beyond the training distribution.

Good analysis beyond headline numbers: retention of general VQA ability (Table 4), multi-task synergy experiments with a cross-dataset transfer argument (Table 5), scaling trends in data and model size (Fig. 4), and a preliminary 'Hard distractor' study probing capacity-dependent learning (Table 6).

Practical application demonstrated: multi-frame reward annotation for robotics with out-of-distribution robot-arm scenes, a plausible and novel use case enabled specifically by multi-frame capability.

Supplementary material is substantive: full sampling algorithm, rotation-angle derivations, code listings for the BFS search and rigid body segmentation, and per-task data samples/templates, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Domain narrowness: all data derives from only three indoor scene sources (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio via TAPVid3D). Claims about multi-frame spatial understanding are supported only on indoor, largely static-object environments; generalization to outdoor, driving, or more dynamic real-world scenes is untested.

The benchmark is generated by the same templated pipeline as the training data. Although eval scenes are held out, question templates, distractor generation, and answer conventions are shared, so the evaluation partially rewards template/format fitting rather than general spatial reasoning. The very low baseline scores on quantitative tasks (near 0 for vectors) partly reflect unfamiliar answer formats, and the use of extra prompts plus GPT-4 post-processing for proprietary models may understate their true ability.

A significant fraction of the claimed 27M samples is unused: training uses only 3M samples ('due to computational constraints'), so the paper's headline dataset scale is not fully validated by experiments, and there is no ablation on how much data beyond 3M would help except for the single camera-vector task in Fig. 4.

The 'emergence' claim (Sec. 4.3) is thin: it rests on one task, three model sizes, and a confounded comparison (the 13B variant has a much larger vision encoder but smaller LLM than the 26B), making it hard to attribute the jump to LLM capacity alone. The authors acknowledge this, but the claim is prominent in the abstract/introduction.

Metric sensitivity: correctness thresholds (20% relative L2 error for scalars/vectors, 5% image width for pixels) are reasonable but somewhat arbitrary, and accuracy on fine-grained regression-style tasks (e.g., 12.92% on object movement vectors) is presented without per-task error statistics (mean/median error) that would better characterize progress on unsolved tasks.

Only two-frame scenarios are used in most experiments despite the paper's multi-frame framing; the data engine supports more views but this remains future work, weakening the 'multi-frame' generalization story for >2 frames.

Several presentation issues: template typos in the data (e.g., 'perform.' in Listing 4/Fig. 6), apparent inconsistency between Fig. 1's example answer ('the point at [472,148] is closer' under Depth Perception) and its stated question, and the correspondence field/project page left blank, which hurts verifiability of dataset release and reproducibility at review time.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: multi-frame spatial understanding for MLLMs, going beyond prior single-image efforts (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT). MultiSPA appears to be the first large-scale dataset dedicated to this, with 27M+ QA samples spanning depth, correspondence, camera/object motion, and object size.

The data engine is well-conceived: leveraging aligned 3D/4D sources (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio/TAPVid3D), back-projecting point clouds to establish ground-truth correspondences, balanced sampling across overlap and motion-magnitude bins, rigid-body segmentation, and a BFS-based minimum-coverage-set search for object size data. The supplementary listings make the pipeline concrete and reproducible.
The benchmark supports diverse output formats (qualitative, MCQ, scalar, coordinate, vector) and unified metrics, which is more informative than MCQ-only benchmarks like BLINK or UniQA-3D.

Experiments cover meaningful questions: absolute gains over base and proprietary models (Table 2), transfer to BLINK (Table 3, +26.4% average), retention of general VQA ability (Table 4), multi-task synergy with a controlled ScanNet-only transfer experiment (Table 5), a data/model scaling study (Fig. 4), and a preliminary 'emergence' analysis (Table 6).
The paper is clearly written, tasks are precisely defined with explicit axis conventions and rotation formulas, and limitations (two-view only, preliminary emergence claims) are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Self-referential evaluation is the central weakness. The benchmark samples are generated by the same data engine, from the same source datasets (ScanNet, TAPVid3D-derived ADT/PStudio), with the same templates and coordinate conventions as training data. The paper asserts scene-level separation and 300 held-out samples per subtask (7,800 total), but distribution, template style, and annotation procedures remain identical to training. High accuracy (e.g., 80-90% on qualitative tasks) may partly reflect template/format familiarity rather than genuine spatial capability; the 20% relative error tolerance for scalars is also generous. Only the BLINK evaluation (4 splits) tests truly out-of-pipeline data.

Baseline comparisons are asymmetric: the proposed model is fine-tuned on MultiSPA while all baselines, including 13B/26B InternVL and proprietary models, are evaluated zero-shot. Fair comparisons would include baselines fine-tuned on comparable spatial data (e.g., SAT, SpatialVLM-style data) or an ablation showing the gain is not simply from multi-image instruction tuning on any data.

Despite the 'multi-frame' framing, nearly all experiments use only two views; object size perception uses at most two images due to search cost. This limits the claimed contribution to pairwise reasoning, and the limitation is deferred to future work.

Source-domain diversity is narrow: ScanNet (indoor scans), PStudio (lab light stage), and ADT (indoor egocentric). Claims of generalizable spatial understanding rest heavily on BLINK transfer, and the robotics 'reward annotator' demonstration (Fig. 5) is a single qualitative example on one scenario with no quantitative evaluation, so its evidential value is limited.

The 'emergent abilities' claim is preliminary and potentially overstated: it is based on one task (MCQ visual correspondence), three model sizes, and a shift from random to near-distractor points, which could reflect task difficulty/data quantity rather than genuine emergence. The authors acknowledge this, but the section title overstates the evidence.
Only 3M of the 27M samples are used for training due to compute constraints, so the headline dataset scale is not fully validated; the scalability study (Fig. 4) covers a single hard subtask.

Reproducibility: correspondence and project-page fields are blank in the manuscript, and only a subset of templates appears in the appendix (the rest deferred to a website), which hinders independent verification of the data engine at present.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending MLLM spatial understanding from single images to multi-frame reasoning is a meaningful gap, and the paper frames it around three concrete capabilities (depth, correspondence, dynamic perception).

Substantial data contribution: MultiSPA (27M+ QA samples from 1.1M images) is claimed to be the first large-scale multi-frame spatial dataset; the data engine (overlap-ratio-based pair sampling, balanced binning, point-cloud backprojection for GT correspondence, rigid-body segmentation for dynamic data) is carefully designed and reasonably well documented, including code listings in the appendix.

Comprehensive evaluation: large gains over InternVL2 baselines of multiple sizes and over proprietary models (Claude-3.5, Gemini-2.0, GPT-4o) on the proposed benchmark, with a credible average improvement of ~36 points on an 8B model.

Generalization is tested beyond the self-proposed benchmark: strong zero-shot gains on BLINK (e.g., 89.5 on Visual Correspondence, 94.7 on Multi-View Reasoning) support transferability of the learned spatial abilities, mitigating the concern of template/domain overfitting.
Retention of general VQA capability (Tab. 4) is checked, addressing the common failure mode of fine-tuned spatial models losing general-purpose skills.

Useful analyses: multi-task synergy experiments (Tab. 5) with a clean cross-dataset transfer argument, a scaling study over data size and model size (Fig. 4), and an exploratory 'hard-task emergence' study (Tab. 6) that is honest about being preliminary.
Novel application angle: demonstrating the model as a multi-frame reward annotator for robotics is a compelling downstream use case supported by a zero-shot OOD demonstration.
Limitations are acknowledged (two-view scenarios, unclear drivers of emergence).
weaknesses: Benchmark/data circularity: the MultiSPA benchmark is generated by the same pipeline, templates, and source datasets (ScanNet, TAPVid3D/ADT/PStudio) as the training data; held-out scenes help, but the evaluation may partly reward learning template and answer-format patterns rather than genuine spatial reasoning. External validation rests mainly on a four-split subset of BLINK.
Small evaluation sets: only 300 samples per subtask (7,800 total) makes per-subtask numbers noisy, especially for the hardest tasks where differences of a few points are interpreted.

Generous metrics: a 20% relative L2 tolerance for scalars/vectors and 5%-width tolerance for pixel coordinates weaken the evidential value of quantitative-output results; no comparison to stricter tolerances or continuous-error metrics is reported.

Domain narrowness: all source data are indoor scenes (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio); claims of 'generalizable multi-frame reasoning' are not tested on outdoor, egocentric-beyond-ADT, or in-the-wild multi-frame imagery, and the sim/annotation-quality caveat the authors raise about prior work applies to their reliance on dataset-provided depth/poses as well.

Proprietary-model comparison involves answer-elicitation prompts and GPT-4-based post-processing, which could introduce format-related bias; details of these prompts are not given in the main text, and the exact-matching/regex extraction may disadvantage models that answer correctly but verbosely.

Only 3M of the 27M samples are actually used for training due to compute constraints, so the headline dataset scale is not fully validated by the main results; the scalability claim is supported only via the camera-vector case study.

The 'emergence' claim is weakly supported: a single task, three model sizes, and no control for encoder resolution/other confounds; the authors appropriately hedge, but the framing could overstate the finding.
Two-frame only: despite the 'multi-frame' title, nearly all experiments use image pairs; genuinely longer-horizon temporal reasoning remains untested.

Reproducibility concerns: correspondence and project page fields are blank in the manuscript, and while the pipeline is described at a high level (with simplified listings), full release of the 27M-sample dataset and exact benchmark scripts is asserted but not verifiable from the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: multi-frame spatial understanding in MLLMs, whereas prior spatial-training work (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT) is confined to single images. The core claim that single-image spatial supervision does not transfer to multi-image tasks is supported empirically (SpatialRGPT underperforms zero-shot InternVL on MultiSPA).

The MultiSPA dataset (27M+ QA samples from 1.1M images) is a substantial resource built on high-quality ground truth (ScanNet, ADT, PStudio via TAPVid3D) rather than noisy off-the-shelf depth/detector annotations. The data engine — visible-point backprojection, overlap-ratio-based balanced pair sampling, rigid-body segmentation, and BFS minimum-coverage-set search — is technically sound and well described, with code listings and templates in the supplementary material.
Diverse referencing (visual dots, pixel coordinates, semantic labels) and output formats (qualitative, MCQ, scalar, 2D coordinates, 3D vectors) go beyond prior datasets, broadening applicability.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough: the main benchmark with many baselines (open models, SpatialRGPT, Claude-3.5, Gemini-2.0, GPT-4o), scalability studies over data volume/model size, held-out generalization on BLINK and rendered 3RScan scenes, retention of general VQA ability plus a forgetting-curve analysis, multi-task synergy ablations (Tabs. 5, 12, 13), comparison to expert models (VGGT, Depth-Anything, LoFTR), and a zero-shot robotics demonstration.

The multi-task synergy findings (e.g., camera-movement accuracy rising from 9.3% to 18.0% with off-task data from a disjoint dataset) and the preliminary emergent-behavior observation (only the 26B model learns from Hard correspondence samples) are interesting scientific insights beyond the raw resource contribution.
weaknesses: Training and evaluation are dominated by two-frame pairs from only three source datasets (indoor ScanNet scenes, lab PStudio, indoor ADT egocentric video). The MultiSPA benchmark is generated by the same pipeline and template distribution as the training data, so in-domain gains (Tab. 2) partly measure format compliance; the external BLINK/3RScan evaluations mitigate but do not fully remove this concern. Scene diversity beyond indoors is untested.

The 'emergent behavior' claim (Sec. 4.3) is weakly supported: the 8B/13B/26B comparison confounds LLM size with vision-encoder size, only one task is studied, and the authors themselves call it preliminary. This framing risks overclaiming.

The scalar/vector correctness criterion (relative error ≤ 20%) and the 5% pixel tolerance are somewhat lenient; per-task difficulty calibration and sensitivity analysis of the threshold are not provided.

Proprietary baselines rely on prompting to force answers plus GPT-4 post-processing for format extraction; while the effort is reasonable, this introduces an evaluation asymmetry relative to the fine-tuned model that is difficult to audit.

No empirical comparison with the closest concurrent multi-frame work (SAT [54]) — the paper only contrasts data characteristics qualitatively — and the model choices (InternVL2-8B base, LoRA r=16, 3M-sample subset) leave some settings underexplored in the main text, though ablations (Tab. 8) partially compensate.
The paper does not explicitly state whether the dataset, benchmark, or code will be released; for a resource-centric contribution this materially affects community value and reproducibility.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('capabilies', 'ANSWER_TEMPATES'), an incomplete sentence in a supplementary data sample ('Given an image and a specific point's 2D coordinates, perform.'), and the object size task relies on axis-aligned 3D bounding boxes, whose height/width/length semantics are only loosely defined for arbitrary objects.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing spatial-understanding efforts for MLLMs (SpatialVLM, SpatialRGPT) are confined to single images, while multi-frame spatial reasoning is essential for robotics and embodied applications. Table 1 convincingly positions MultiSPA as the first large-scale multi-frame spatial dataset.

The data generation pipeline is technically sound and well documented. Backprojecting aligned point clouds to establish pixel correspondences (Eq. 2-3), overlap-ratio-based pair sampling (Eq. 4) with binning to counteract long-tailed distributions, and clustering-based rigid body segmentation are reasonable, and the appendix (Listings 1-4, BFS coverage search) provides substantial reproducibility detail.

The experimental evidence is broad: large gains on the proposed benchmark (avg. 56.11 vs. 20-30 for baselines including GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude), zero-shot transfer to BLINK (Table 3, +26.4% over base model, e.g., 94.7 on Multi-View Reasoning), preserved general VQA ability (Tables 4, 11), forgetting-curve analysis (Fig. 6), and comparisons against specialized models (VGGT, Depth-Anything, LoFTR) rather than only MLLM baselines.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: scalability with data/model size (Fig. 4), ablations over fine-tuning strategies showing vision-encoder tuning matters (Table 8), and multi-task synergy experiments (Tables 5, 12, 13) that include useful controls (cross-dataset transfer from ScanNet to PStudio/ADT sources).
weaknesses: Potential benchmark circularity: the MultiSPA benchmark is generated with the same pipeline, source datasets, and QA templates as the training data (Sec. 3.3 uses ScanNet and TAPVid3D with the same generation procedure). Although scenes are held out, the large gains on MultiSPA may partly reflect familiarity with question formats and answer conventions rather than genuine spatial competence. The strongest evidence against this is BLINK/ERQA transfer, but those gains are concentrated on a few splits.

Evaluation metrics are coarse: a prediction is correct within 20% relative error (scalars/vectors) or 5% image width (coordinates). This tolerance choice is not justified or ablated, and makes the near-zero baseline scores on vector tasks hard to interpret; a finer-grained error analysis (median error distributions) would strengthen the claims.

The 'emergence' claim (Sec. 4.3, Table 6) is thin: it is based on a single task, a single evaluation setting, three model configurations, and no repeated runs or error bars; the authors themselves label it preliminary. The framing in the abstract overstates what is shown.

Proprietary baselines were prompted to guess and post-processed with GPT-4 for format compliance; while the authors explain this, it introduces an uncontrolled evaluation variable, and no details are given on how consistently this recovers valid answers.

Coverage limitations: training is restricted to indoor scenes from ScanNet/PStudio/ADT and, in the main results, two-frame inputs; the robotics demonstration (Fig. 5) is qualitative with a single example and no quantitative evaluation of the reward-annotator claim.
No explicit statement about releasing the dataset, benchmark, or code, which matters given that dataset contribution is the core claim.

Minor presentation issues: Figure 1 examples show some answers that appear inconsistent with their questions (e.g., a desk-height question answered with a length value), and several typos ('an sampled image pair', 'ANSWER_TEMPATES', 'capabilies') suggest a rushed proofread.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored capability—multi-frame (as opposed to single-image) spatial understanding in MLLMs—and frames it clearly through three fundamental skills (depth perception, visual correspondence, dynamic perception), drawing a sensible analogy to the Structure-from-Motion pipeline.

MultiSPA is a substantial and well-engineered contribution: a scalable data engine built on ScanNet, ADT, PStudio/TAPVid3D that back-projects spatially and temporally aligned point clouds to generate high-quality ground-truth QA pairs at scale (27M+ samples, 1.1M images), supporting diverse referencing (dots, coordinates, semantic labels) and output formats (qualitative, scalar, coordinates, vectors). The appendix details (bin sampling, BFS minimum-coverage-set search, rigid-body segmentation, templates) support reproducibility of the pipeline.

The experimental evidence is broad and convincing: large gains on the MultiSPA benchmark (+35.68 average over InternVL-8B, beating proprietary models), zero-shot transfer to held-out BLINK (+26.4% over base, ~90% on M.V./V.C.), robustness to additional frames (Table 14), retention of general VQA ability with an explicit forgetting-curve analysis (Fig. 6), and comparisons against expert models (VGGT, Depth-Anything, LoFTR).

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: scalability across data volume, model capacity, and trainable parameters (Fig. 4, Table 8); multi-task synergy demonstrated with careful controls (e.g., cross-dataset transfer from ScanNet-only auxiliary data to PStudio/ADT object movement in Table 5; subset ablations in Tables 12-13); and an interesting preliminary finding that only the 26B model learns from 'Hard' correspondence data.

The paper is well organized and clearly written; the benchmark introduces a unified metric across heterogeneous output types, and the potential robotics application (multi-frame reward annotation) is a motivating demonstration on out-of-distribution data.
weaknesses: Domain diversity of the data is limited: all training and benchmark data derive from indoor ScanNet scenes, light-stage PStudio sequences, and indoor ADT egocentric video. Claims of 'generalizable multi-frame perception' rest heavily on this narrow distribution; the 3RScan synthetic test partially mitigates this but is rendered from the same kind of indoor scenes.

The MultiSPA benchmark is generated with the same templates and pipeline as the training data. Although scenes are held out, the template/answer-style overlap means strong benchmark numbers partly measure template adherence; the generality of the learned skill to differently phrased queries is not directly tested.

Baseline results are likely depressed by format-following issues: proprietary models are prompted to guess and post-processed with GPT-4, yet still score near zero on coordinate/vector tasks. The relative-margin claim ('36% gain') is therefore sensitive to these protocol choices, and the 20% relative-error threshold for scalar/vector correctness is somewhat arbitrary.

The 'emergence' claim (Sec. 4.3) is overstated relative to the evidence: it derives from a single task (MCQ visual correspondence), small evaluation sets (300 samples per subtask), and a one-point comparison across three model sizes; alternative explanations (e.g., threshold effects in the metric, training instability at small scale) are not ruled out. The authors appropriately hedge, but the framing in the abstract is stronger.

Despite the title's 'Multi-Frame' emphasis, training data are essentially two-frame pairs; only object-size perception uses multiple images, and generalization to more frames is shown only qualitatively via intermediate-frame insertion. The benchmark samples per subtask (300) are small, limiting statistical precision.

The headline 27M dataset is not actually used at that scale for training (3M subset, LoRA-rank-16 on the LLM only), so the paper's strongest scalability conclusions about the full dataset remain partly speculative; the best 26B fully fine-tuned model on the mixed set could not be trained due to compute limits.

Reproducibility depends on releasing the dataset, benchmark, and code; the paper does not explicitly commit to public release, which is important given that the central contribution is a data/benchmark artifact.
